definition: TODO: A walk with no repeated edges; vertices may repeat
TODO: A walk with no repeated vertices, so no repeated edges either
TODO: A trail that starts and ends at the same vertex: closed, with no repeated edges
TODO: A closed walk with no repeated vertices except the start and end vertex
TODO: A vertex of odd degree; every graph has an even number of odd vertices
TODO: A trail using every edge exactly once; a connected graph has one when it has 0 or 2 odd vertices, and with 2 it must start at one and end at the other
TODO: A circuit using every edge exactly once; a connected graph has one exactly when every vertex has even degree
TODO: A path visiting every vertex exactly once; there is no simple test for whether one exists
TODO: A cycle visiting every vertex exactly once and returning to the start
TODO: A subgraph that is a tree and includes every vertex of the graph
TODO: A spanning tree of least total weight in a connected weighted graph; it may not be unique
TODO: Builds a minimum spanning tree by adding edges in increasing order of weight, skipping any that would make a cycle, until there are n − 1 edges
TODO: Builds a minimum spanning tree from a starting vertex by repeatedly adding the least-weight edge from a tree vertex to a vertex not yet in the tree; also works on a table (matrix method)
TODO: Find the least-weight closed route along every edge at least once; with odd vertices, repeat the least-weight pairing of the odd vertices (up to four in IB)
TODO: Find the least-weight Hamiltonian cycle in a weighted complete graph; practical problems first need a table of least distances
TODO: A table of the shortest route between every pair of vertices, which turns a practical problem into the classical TSP on a complete graph
TODO: From a start vertex go to the nearest unvisited vertex each time, then return to the start; gives an upper bound for the TSP, not necessarily the best tour
TODO: Delete a vertex, find a minimum spanning tree of the rest, add the two least-weight edges from the deleted vertex; gives a lower bound for the TSP, and the largest such bound is the best
